issues.issue: The Bank is defined as "Wells Fargo Bank Minnesota, N.A., or it's agent", so it is unclear whether obligations of "the Bank" run to the named bank alone or also to any agent it uses. The stray possessive "it's" and the garbled date line compound the uncertainty about who is bound.

The preamble dates the agreement the 31st day of January 2001, while Section 14 leaves the effective date blank and the signature block bears "7/6/2000". A court could be asked to reconcile those dates.

The recital defines "Borrower" as "selected brokerage firms and other borrowing organizations", a general catch-all after a single enumerated specific, leaving the class of eligible borrowers uncertain. Section 2(b) then expands "Borrower" to include any affiliate, which the recital does not signal.

The appointment depends on unidentified "other agreements" under which the Bank is custodian and which "authorize Participant to appoint an agent"; the scope of the Account and of the authority conferred can only be determined from documents outside this instrument. Whether those custody agreements' terms qualify this appointment is left open.

The permitted-investment list ends with the general catch-all "and other short term money market instruments", so the reach of that phrase against the enumerated specifics (repos, treasuries, CDs, bankers acceptances, commercial paper) is exactly the ejusdem generis question a collateral-investment loss would raise. "Short term" is itself unbounded, and the Bank's own "policy and standard guidelines established from time to time" are given power to define the permitted universe.

The Bank's unilateral "policy and standard guidelines" power sits awkwardly against Section 8, which places all collateral investment loss on the Participant while allowing the Bank to set the investment parameters. Harmonising the two leaves it unclear whether breach of the list is a Bank risk or a Participant risk.

"The prime considerations ... shall be safety of principal and liquidity requirements" is a standard without a benchmark: "prime considerations" may be read as a binding investment mandate or as mere hortatory guidance, and "liquidity requirements" is nowhere specified. The term cannot be applied to any concrete investment without construction.

This safety-of-principal duty is hard to square with Section 8, under which the Participant "assumes all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss". One provision imposes an investment standard on the Bank while the other allocates the resulting loss entirely to the Participant.

"Reasonable efforts to allocate loans on a security by security queue basis" is undefined, and the queue mechanism is nowhere described. The clause then concedes a single Borrower may receive all of the Participant's securities, leaving the allocation obligation with no measurable content.

The recital that the Program "is designed to allocate securities loans equitably among the Participants" points toward an equitable-allocation duty that this operative text substantially disclaims. A court could be asked whether the recital qualifies the "reasonable efforts" standard.

The unconditional duty to return collateral to the Borrower sits against the closing sentence of Section 4 giving the Bank "a reasonable time ... to liquidate cash collateral investments", and against Section 8's allocation of collateral investment loss. Timing and shortfall consequences are not reconciled.

The entitlement runs to "cash dividends, stock dividends, stock splits, rights of distribution, conversion privileges, tender and exchange offers, and similar corporate actions", a catch-all whose reach beyond the listed items is uncertain. "Notice ... from the proper party" is likewise undefined.

"Net earnings from each loan" is undefined, so whether losses on the pooled cash collateral are netted before the 40/60 split — and how pooled income is attributed to "each loan" — cannot be determined from the words. The clause also shifts between "net earnings" and "fees" without distinguishing them.

The Bank's 40% share of collateral-investment earnings is difficult to reconcile with Section 8, which places all collateral investment loss on the Participant alone. A court could be asked whether the profit-sharing arrangement qualifies that one-sided loss allocation.

"Participant assumes all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss" states an unqualified assumption of risk with no carve-out on its face, yet "all risk of loss" must somehow accommodate the Bank's own conduct. Whether it covers losses caused by the Bank's investment decisions is precisely the open term.

It cannot be squared with the closing sentence of the same Section 8, under which "The Bank assumes the risk of loss arising from negligent and fraudulent operation of its Securities Lending Program", nor with Section 2(f)'s safety-of-principal mandate. One sentence gives the Participant all investment loss, the other gives the Bank losses from its own negligent operation.

"Negligent and fraudulent operation" is conjunctive as written, so it can be read to require both negligence and fraud before the Bank bears any loss, and "operation of its Securities Lending Program" does not say whether investment of cash collateral is "operation". The mis-typed conjunction changes the scope of the Bank's assumed risk.

It directly contradicts the opening sentence of Section 8, which gives the Participant "all risk of loss arising out of ... collateral investment loss", leaving no rule for a collateral investment loss caused by negligent Bank operation. The two sentences of the same section allocate the identical loss to opposite parties.

The waiver sentence is internally inconsistent: it conditions waiver on "mutual agreement" yet says "either party may waive all or part of the Notice period", so it is unclear whether waiver is unilateral or bilateral. Termination is also made subject to the Borrower Security Loan Agreements, which are not part of this instrument.

The notice address names "Copic Companies" while the contracting party is "Copic Insurance Company", a discrepancy in the identity of the notice recipient. The clause also prescribes mailing only, with no timing or deemed-receipt rule.

Excluding headings from construction cuts against reliance on the heading "Risk of Loss" and similar labels used to organise Sections 2, 4 and 8, which parties would otherwise invoke to harmonise the conflicting risk sentences. The practical effect of the exclusion on those sections could be argued.

The clause says the Agreement is "binding on the successors and assigns" without saying whether assignment is permitted or requires consent, so it can be read either as authorising assignment or merely as binding permitted assigns. The unaddressed assignment right is the ambiguity.
The effective date is left blank ("on the ___ day of January, 2001"), so the instrument does not state when it takes effect. That omission is a mechanical defect that changes when obligations began.

It cannot be squared with the preamble, which dates the agreement the 31st day of January 2001, or with the execution date "7/6/2000" in the signature block. A court would have to choose among three inconsistent dates.
